name: Heteropogon
look_here_first: TANGLEHEAD (the only Heteropogon currently installed in our learner) is an erect perennial bunchgrass with usually narrow one-sided flowering racemes. Watch its SEASONAL sequence: closely appressed green spikelet units and hairs, remarkably long often 5–8 cm dark bent or twisted fertile AWNS, and eventually the AWNS becoming intertwined at the top of the raceme. Confirm a fertile SESSILE and sterile/pedicelled companion spikelet, plus its exceedingly SHARP hairy basal CALLUS under hand lens. Do not claim a Hays specimen or callus/ligule measurement from the available wide photographs.

recognition.where_to_look_first: Start at one flowering raceme, not the brown bunch: separate green raceme units from long dark awns and finally mature intertwined awns.
priority: 3 source-identified existing physical photo stages: early green rachis, dark awned flowering axis, upright bunch habit
One clearly credited external mature tangled-awns photo from South Africa, CC BY-SA 2.0 (not local voucher)
True attached fertile sessile + pedicelled companion spikelet macro, millimeter sharp bearded callus
True 1-mm fringed/ciliate ligule and whole attached root crown
recognition.warning: Long dark awns strongly favor tanglehead in local grass comparisons, but the source photo alone does not prove a local species determination. No invented microscopic arrows.

comparison_lesson.title: Tanglehead versus KR bluestem, silver bluestem, little bluestem and old world bluestems
comparison_lesson.memory_rule: Tanglehead = narrow spike + LONG DARK twisted/bent awns, later often tangled. VERIFY PAIR and the very SHARP bearded callus.
quick_split: KR bluestem, Bothriochloa ischaemum: clustered shorter/radiating racemes, less dramatic long-dark-awns spire; compare actual adult flowering architecture.
Silver bluestem, Bothriochloa laguroides: conspicuously pale/silver hairy reproductive branches; usually shorter awns and different panicle layout.
Little bluestem, Schizachyrium scoparium: many fluffy/silvery seed-bearing branches, not one narrowly concentrated dark-awns tangle.
Old-world bluestems Dichanthium (introduced): different multiple/radiating heads and awn/spikelet pair characters, never infer exotic status solely from hairiness.
comparison_lesson.guardrail: These are visual comparison taxa, not newly installed Heteropogon species or county-native certifications. The original CC BY-NC image remains noncommercial; CC BY-SA sources require attribution/share alike.

comparisons.field_cues: Source-verified image sequence: green appressed rachis and pale hairs → very long dark twisted fertile awns → mature intertwined tangle, with an erect bunch habit.
comparisons.lookalikes_and_split: Bothriochloa KR/silver differ in overall flowering head architecture and shorter awns; Schizachyrium in fluffy silvery spikelet tufts; Dichanthium in radiating short racemes. Complete ID requires sessile fertile/pedicelled spikelet pair and very sharp hairy basal callus.

what_to_teach_crew: Look for a thin unilateral flowering raceme, not a broad branched panicle.
Trace one very long dark twisted awn to a fertile spikelet on the axis; a photo containing many strands cannot prove individual lengths.
Know immature green spikelet units BEFORE mature tangles develop. The early photo does not show a mature tangle.
Under hand lens find the paired fertile sessile and pedicelled companion, and inspect the sharp hairy callus (spiky seed, handle carefully).
Distinguish local Bothriochloa, Schizachyrium and Dichanthium seedheads by branching and awn layout, not brown color.
visual_needs: One source-confirmed wild Hays-area complete root-to-mature flowering shoot with species vouchers and scale.
Attached sessile fertile plus pedicelled companion spikelet pair in ONE real 10–20× macro; don't guess floral sex from source wide photo.
Very sharp bearded 2–3 mm basal callus and whole 5–8 cm dark twisted awn in a mm-scaled attached mature example.
Fine leaf–sheath collar and fringed/ciliate ligule 10–20×, not visible in existing images.
Photo-level license version check for original GBIF/iNat archived shots when available, plus public mobile arrow QA.
External Bernard Dupont licensed CC BY-SA mature intertwined-awns panel may be physically archived after proper EXIF/rights QA; current source is a remotely served provisional review.

visual_comparison.title: Tanglehead — green spike → long dark awns → tangled maturity
visual_comparison.subtitle: One installed tanglehead species: 3 physically stored/inspected credited source photographs plus 1 Bernard DUPONT external CC BY-SA 2.0 mature-tangle photo; 7 conservative visible-region arrows. Species ID and original photo-rights restrictions preserved.
visual_comparison.memory_rule: LONG, dark TWISTED awns on a narrow raceme → a mature tangle. Confirm an attached fertile sessile spikelet plus pedicelled companion and its sharp hairy callus.

items.label: 1 · GREEN RACEME — overlapping units and pale hairs
items.image_role: Earlier-stage source-identified narrow green flowering raceme showing overlapping green units and fine pale hairs against the photographer's hand
items.caption: The original archived photograph shows green overlapping spikelet-scale parts and fine pale hairs on the narrow axis. Some purplish/pale exserted floral structures are visible, but their precise sex/attachments are not securely resolved. A mature awn tangle is NOT pictured here.
items.why_it_matters: See how a younger tanglehead looks before dark mature awns become prominent.
items.photo_status: Physically verified original CC BY-NC image; noncommercial credit required; PROVISIONAL species/source photo review, no microanatomy claims.

items.creator: Nathan Aaron
items.label: 2 · FLOWERING HEADS — long dark awns
items.image_role: Source-determined paired upright narrow tanglehead racemes with long dark awns above green spikelet-bearing axes
items.caption: Original Nathan Aaron photograph shows two upright narrow flowering axes, dark elongated awn portions above, and exserted purple/pale floral structures lower down. Awn tips extend out of frame, so neither total length nor the sharp basal callus can be measured.
items.why_it_matters: Compare long dark awns with shorter-awns bluestem heads; do not identify from color alone.
items.photo_status: Original source CC BY archived JPEG reinspected at pixel level 2026-10-21; gross awn/raceme arrows only.

items.creator: Susan Brown
items.label: 3 · HABIT — erect, dense late-season bunchgrass
items.image_role: Wide source-identified dry yellow-green tanglehead bunch and stems, no visible diagnostic individual floret
items.caption: Original Susan Brown image shows many upright straw-colored flowering stems and thin leaves in closely massed bunches. A single root crown, ligule and attached mature spikelet pair are not resolvable.
items.why_it_matters: Whole-plant growth form supports identification alongside the distinctive flowering head, not instead of it.
items.photo_status: Physically inspected CC BY-SA archived source with original attribution and share-alike requirement; source determination provisional, license version still to be independently checked.

items.label: 4 · MATURE — tangled dark awns (South African reference)

items.caption: Bernard Dupont's CC BY-SA 2.0 image shows a tangle of long slender dark awns among flowering grass stems. It cannot demonstrate a local Hays occurrence, the tiny basal callus or a precisely measured fertile spikelet.
items.why_it_matters: Shows the genus's memorable mature TANGLE not yet present in our three archived local-source photographs.

study_only_photo_links.label: Heteropogon contortus botanical reference
study_only_photo_links.look_for: TANGLEHEAD: native warm-season perennial tuft whose tightly clustered fertile florets bear extraordinarily LONG TWISTED or bent dark awns, which eventually TANGLE together as seedheads mature. Look for the paired sessile and pedicelled spikelets under 10× and the pale hairy raceme around them. A fresh un-tangled head can still be diagnostic from its long awns.
